name: FOUNDATION
label: Month 1 · Async + FastAPI + raw LLM APIs
goal: Call any provider directly: tool use, structured output, streaming. No frameworks.

weeks.title: Async Python for IO-bound work
weeks.why: Django taught you synchronous, ORM-first thinking. Every LLM call is IO-bound and slow (300ms-30s). The single biggest latency win in LLM engineering is doing calls concurrently. Interviewers probe this because it separates people who read tutorials from people who shipped.

tasks.t: Understand the event loop: coroutines, await, why async is NOT threads, and why one blocking call freezes everything
asyncio.gather vs asyncio.TaskGroup (3.11+). Use TaskGroup — gather's error semantics will bite you.
asyncio.Semaphore for rate limiting. Every provider rate-limits you; this is how you respect it.
httpx.AsyncClient — connection pooling, timeouts, retries. Stop using requests.
The blocking trap: asyncio.to_thread / run_in_executor for CPU or sync-DB work inside an async app
async context managers and async generators (you need these for streaming next week)
BUILD: fire 50 LLM calls concurrently with a Semaphore(5), exponential backoff on 429, print p50/p95 latency and total wall time. Compare against the sequential version.

resources.label: FastAPI — Concurrency and async/await (the best plain-English explanation there is)

Super Fast Python — asyncio guide (free, exhaustive reference)

code.label: The pattern you will use for the next 6 months
code.body:
import asyncio, time, httpx

SEM = asyncio.Semaphore(5)          # respect the rate limit

async def call(client, prompt):
    async with SEM:
        for attempt in range(4):
            r = await client.post(URL, json={"prompt": prompt}, timeout=60)
            if r.status_code != 429:
                return r.json()
            await asyncio.sleep(2 ** attempt)   # exponential backoff
        raise RuntimeError("rate limited out")

async def main(prompts):
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    async with httpx.AsyncClient() as client:
        async with asyncio.TaskGroup() as tg:    # 3.11+, better errors than gather
            tasks = [tg.create_task(call(client, p)) for p in prompts]
    print(f"{len(prompts)} calls in {time.perf_counter()-t0:.1f}s")
    return [t.result() for t in tasks]

weeks.deliverable: A benchmark script showing sequential vs concurrent wall time for 50 calls. Screenshot the numbers — you will quote them in an interview.
weeks.checkpoint: Why does `time.sleep(1)` inside an async function destroy your throughput, but `await asyncio.sleep(1)` does not?

labs.title: asyncio — the three files you wrote
labs.note: Your own code, kept read-only. This is the reference you come back to in Week 4 when the tool loop needs to fire calls concurrently.

tabs.name: TaskGroup
tabs.note: Three ways to run coroutines concurrently — and why only one of them fails safely. create_task orphans siblings on error; gather propagates but leaves them running; TaskGroup cancels the group and raises an ExceptionGroup. Structured concurrency.
tabs.body:
import asyncio

async def fetch_data(name, delay):
    print(f"Starting task {name}")
    await asyncio.sleep(delay)
    print(f"Finished task {name}")
    return f"Result of task {name}"


async def main():
    # we can start run each task concurrently via 
    # 1. first approach -> 
    # task1 = asyncio.create_task(fetch_data("Task 1", 1))
    # task2 = asyncio.create_task(fetch_data("Task 2", 2))
    # task3 = asyncio.create_task(fetch_data("Task 3", 3))

    # 2. second approach -> [gather]
    # result = await asyncio.gather(fetch_data("Task 1", 1), fetch_data("Task 2", 2), fetch_data("Task 3", 3))
    # print(result)

    #3rd approad [Task group]
    tasks =[]
    async with asyncio.TaskGroup() as tg:
        for i , sleep_time in enumerate([1, 2, 3], start  = 1 ):
            task = tg.create_task(fetch_data(i, sleep_time))
            tasks.append(task)

    results = [task.result() for task in tasks]
    print(results)

# Approach 1 (asyncio.create_task manually): if task2 raises an exception, nothing automatically cancels task1/task3 or even surfaces the error unless you explicitly await each task and check. Tasks can fail silently — you might never notice unless you happen to await them.
# Approach 2 (asyncio.gather): better, since it does propagate the first exception raised. But by default it does not cancel the other still-running tasks when one fails — they keep running in the background orphaned, unless you pass return_exceptions=True and handle it yourself, which is easy to forget.
# Approach 3 (TaskGroup): if any task inside the group raises, it automatically cancels all the other sibling tasks, waits for them to finish cancelling, and then raises an ExceptionGroup containing everything that failed. It's structured concurrency — no dangling tasks, no silent failures. This is the same idea Trio pioneered and Python later adopted natively.

if __name__ == "__main__":
    asyncio.run(main())

tabs.name: Lock
tabs.note: asyncio.Lock serialises a critical section: five tasks want the shared counter, exactly one gets it at a time. Async code is single-threaded but still interleaves at every await — which is where races appear.
tabs.body:
import asyncio

# A shared lock 
shared_resource = 0

# A async lock 
lock = asyncio.Lock()


# idea is that 5 tasks want to modify the shared_resource at the same time 
# but there will be a lock , so that only 1 task at a time can modify the resource 
async def modify_shared_lock():
    global shared_resource
    async with lock :
        #enterine  
        print('Entering criticle section :[resource before modifiction]' , shared_resource)
        await asyncio.sleep(1)
        shared_resource += 1 
        print('Exit criticle section :[resource after modifiction]' , shared_resource)


async def main ():
    await asyncio.gather(*[modify_shared_lock() for i in range(5)])


if __name__ == "__main__":
    asyncio.run(main())

tabs.name: Semaphore
tabs.note: A Lock of size N. This is the rate limiter you will use against every LLM provider — Semaphore(5) means five requests in flight, the rest queue. Week 1's build task is exactly this.
tabs.body:
# A semaphore is a concurrency-control mechanism that limits how many tasks can access something at the same time.
import asyncio

async def access_resource(semaphore, resource_id):
    async with semaphore:
        # simulate accessing a limited resource 
        print('accessing resource' , resource_id)
        await asyncio.sleep(1)
        print('exiting resource' , resource_id)

async def main():
    semaphore = asyncio.Semaphore(2) # allow 2 concurrent accesses to the resource at a time 
    tasks = [access_resource(semaphore, i) for i in range(5)]
    await asyncio.gather(*tasks)

if __name__ == '__main__':
    asyncio.run(main())

weeks.title: FastAPI properly (mapped from DRF)
weeks.why: You know DRF. FastAPI is not 'Django but smaller' — the dependency injection and Pydantic-first design change how you structure code. Map each DRF concept to its FastAPI equivalent and you will learn this in a week instead of a month.

tasks.t: Pydantic v2: BaseModel, Field, validators, model_validate, model_dump. This is your DRF serializer replacement — and it is also how you get structured output from LLMs.
Path/query/body params, response_model, status codes. Map to DRF: serializer -> Pydantic model, ViewSet -> APIRouter.
Depends() — dependency injection. Use it for auth, DB sessions, and your LLM client. There is no DRF equivalent; learn it properly.
lifespan context manager (load your embedding model ONCE at startup, not per request)
StreamingResponse + SSE. This is how token-by-token output reaches your React Native app.
BackgroundTasks, exception handlers, middleware, CORS (your RN app will need CORS)
BUILD: a FastAPI service with 3 endpoints, one of which streams SSE. Hit the stream from a plain HTML page and watch tokens arrive.

code.label: SSE streaming — the endpoint your mobile app will consume
code.body:
from fastapi import FastAPI
from fastapi.responses import StreamingResponse
from contextlib import asynccontextmanager

@asynccontextmanager
async def lifespan(app: FastAPI):
    app.state.llm = make_client()      # load ONCE, not per request
    yield
    await app.state.llm.aclose()

app = FastAPI(lifespan=lifespan)

async def token_stream(prompt: str):
    async for chunk in app.state.llm.stream(prompt):
        yield f"data: {json.dumps({'t': chunk})}\n\n"   # SSE wire format
    yield "data: [DONE]\n\n"

@app.post("/chat")
async def chat(body: ChatIn):
    return StreamingResponse(token_stream(body.message),
                             media_type="text/event-stream")

weeks.deliverable: A running FastAPI service with a working SSE endpoint, Pydantic-validated request/response, and auto-generated /docs.
weeks.checkpoint: Explain Depends() to someone who only knows Django. What problem does it solve that Django middleware does not?

weeks.title: Raw LLM APIs — no frameworks
weeks.why: LangChain hides exactly the thing you are being hired to understand. Every abstraction you will later use is a wrapper around an HTTP POST with a messages array. Learn the POST.

tasks.t: The messages array: system / user / assistant roles, multi-turn, why context is resent every call (this is why cost scales with conversation length)
Sampling params: temperature, top_p, max_tokens, stop sequences. Know when temperature=0 is wrong.
Structured output — three mechanisms: JSON mode, JSON schema / responseSchema, and tool-forcing. Know which providers support which.
Streaming: parse SSE from the provider, handle partial JSON, handle mid-stream errors
Tokens and cost: tokenizers, counting before you send, cost per 1M in/out, why output tokens cost 3-5x input
Prompt engineering that actually matters: few-shot examples, XML/delimiter structure, chain-of-thought, prefilling the assistant turn
BUILD: llm.py — ONE interface, four providers behind it (Gemini, Groq, OpenRouter, Ollama). Streaming and structured output work identically across all four.

code.label: Structured output via Pydantic — you will use this constantly
code.body:
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field
from typing import Literal

class TicketTriage(BaseModel):
    category: Literal["billing", "bug", "feature", "other"]
    severity: int = Field(ge=1, le=5)
    summary: str = Field(max_length=200)
    needs_human: bool

# Gemini: pass the schema directly
resp = client.models.generate_content(
    model="gemini-2.0-flash",
    contents=ticket_text,
    config={"response_mime_type": "application/json",
            "response_schema": TicketTriage},
)
triage = TicketTriage.model_validate_json(resp.text)   # typed, validated

# THE LESSON: the model returns a string. Pydantic is what makes it data.
# When validation fails, feed the error back to the model and retry. That's
# all any 'structured output library' does.

weeks.deliverable: llm.py — a provider-agnostic module. Swapping Gemini for Groq is a one-line change.
weeks.checkpoint: Your structured-output call returns malformed JSON 5% of the time. Name three ways to fix it, in order of cost.

weeks.title: Tool use / function calling — write the loop yourself
weeks.why: This is the single most important week of Month 1. Agents, MCP, LangGraph, Claude Code, every AI product you admire — all of it is this loop. Once you have written it by hand, no agent framework can confuse you again.

tasks.t: The anatomy: tool schema -> model emits tool_use -> YOU execute -> send tool_result -> model continues. Draw it on paper.
Write the while-loop by hand. No SDK auto-execution. Handle max_iterations to avoid infinite loops.
Parallel tool calls — the model can request several at once. Run them with asyncio (Week 1 pays off here).
Error handling: what do you send back when a tool raises? (Answer: the error message, as a tool_result. The model can often recover.)
Tool design: descriptions are prompts. Rewrite a bad tool description and measure the difference in correct-call rate.
Wire 3 real tools over your Django DB: a filtered query, an aggregate, and a write action with confirmation
MILESTONE: FastAPI streaming chat endpoint + the hand-written tool loop + 3 real tools. This is Project A's backend v0.

Anthropic — Writing effective tools for agents

code.label: The loop. Memorise this shape.
code.body:
async def run(user_msg, tools, max_iters=10):
    messages = [{"role": "user", "content": user_msg}]

    for i in range(max_iters):
        resp = await llm.chat(messages, tools=[t.schema for t in tools])
        messages.append({"role": "assistant", "content": resp.content})

        calls = [b for b in resp.content if b.type == "tool_use"]
        if not calls:
            return resp.text                       # model is done

        # execute requested tools CONCURRENTLY (Week 1 pays off)
        async def exec_one(c):
            try:
                out = await tools[c.name](**c.input)
            except Exception as e:
                out = f"ERROR: {e}"                # errors go back as results
            return {"type": "tool_result", "tool_use_id": c.id, "content": str(out)}

        results = await asyncio.gather(*[exec_one(c) for c in calls])
        messages.append({"role": "user", "content": results})

    raise RuntimeError("hit max iterations")

weeks.deliverable: PROJECT A BACKEND v0 — a streaming FastAPI chat endpoint with a hand-written tool loop over your real database.
